title: Are Worksheets Bad?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Pushing back on the common teacher refrain that "worksheets are the worst," Dave Stuart Jr. argues the real culprit is poor thinking about teaching and learning, not the paper itself, since a worksheet is "an inanimate object." He makes the case through three examples of worksheet-like tools that become powerful instructional resources in the hands of a thoughtful teacher: Doug Stark's Mechanics Instruction that Sticks warm-ups, which function as interactive mini-lessons rather than independent busywork when used as designed; Chris Hulleman and Character Lab's Build Connections exercise, which becomes a vehicle for pair and whole-class discussion about how coursework relates to students' actual lives; and Gabriele Oettingen's WOOP goal-setting worksheet, which he watched move a room of conference participants to tears when facilitated properly. In each case, Stuart contrasts the malpractice version (chucking the sheet at students and disengaging) with the version grounded in understanding the underlying research and method. He closes by generalizing the argument beyond worksheets specifically: sweeping pedagogical slogans provide the illusion of clarity without its substance, and professional development should instead build teachers' genuine understanding of how learning works.
points: Stuart's central reframe is that a worksheet is "an inanimate object" — the deciding factor is always the thinking behind how a teacher uses it, not the paper format itself.

Doug Stark's warm-ups curriculum illustrates the distinction directly: Doug's own instructions warn that "the warm-ups will not work if you use them like worksheets," requiring interactive facilitation.

The Build Connections exercise shows how a single-sided worksheet becomes a discussion engine linking course content like Hamlet or the Han Dynasty to students' actual lives, when a teacher studies the science behind it first.

Witnessing Gabriele Oettingen facilitate WOOP at a 2018 conference — moving participants to tears — is offered as proof that even goal-setting worksheets carry real emotional weight when properly taught.
He generalizes the argument to warn against sweeping pedagogical slogans generally, arguing they provide the illusion of clarity without its substance.
quotes: But — but! — there are instances where things that look an awful lot like worksheets are simply the best and most efficient means through which to achieve a certain instructional goal.

The warm-ups will not work if you use them like worksheets. You can't just hand them out and let the kids go. I try to think of each warm-up as an interactive lesson with multiple checks for understanding.

But in the hands of an earnest teacher who takes the time to read the science and strategies behind this worksheet, this can become a recurring tool for creating pair, small group, and whole-class discussions around how Algebra or Physics or Hamlet or the Han Dynasty relates to students' actual lives.
There were practically tears by the end from multiple participants because it was so beautifully done.

Sweeping statements like "worksheets are the worst," "all books are good books," "desks in rows are terrible…" these provide the illusion of clarity (all over-generalizations do) but not clarity's substance.
